findings.title: Background writes retain the request’s cancellation
findings.description:
All four write methods launch legacy work using `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`, where `ctx` is still derived from the incoming request. The ten-second timeout does not detach cancellation: once the HTTP handler returns, request cancellation can abort the legacy write immediately. Consequently, successful primary writes may routinely fail to reach legacy storage.

Either complete replication before returning or use a background-work lifecycle that preserves required context values without inheriting request cancellation. Add a test that cancels the request after the primary write succeeds and verifies the intended replication behavior.

findings.title: Update recomputes the mutation against the legacy object
findings.description:
The legacy call now receives the original `objInfo` rather than an `updateWrapper` containing the successful storage result. In `pkg/registry/apis/playlist/legacy_storage.go`, `Update` loads the legacy object and calls `objInfo.UpdatedObject(ctx, old)` again.

For patches or other transformations dependent on the existing object, a stale legacy object can produce a different result from the authoritative storage update. Reusing the original transformation can also repeat request-specific processing after the request has completed. Restore replication of the successfully persisted object rather than independently recomputing the mutation.

findings.title: Independent goroutines can replicate writes out of order
findings.description:
Create, Update, and Delete each launch an independent goroutine without sequencing operations for the same resource. Even sequential client requests can therefore be applied to legacy storage in a different order: an update may run before the preceding create, two updates may overwrite each other in reverse order, or a delayed create may resurrect an already-deleted object.

Fixing context cancellation alone will not resolve this. Preserve per-resource write ordering, use version-aware replication, or retain synchronous replication until an ordered mechanism exists. Cover create→update, update→update, and create→delete sequences with deliberately delayed legacy operations.

findings.title: Duration observations use the wrong backend and label
findings.description:
Several observations misrepresent the operations being measured:

- Create and Update record primary-storage failures with `recordLegacyDuration`.
- Delete records the resource `name` in the `kind` label on success.
- DeleteCollection records the legacy operation with `recordStorageDuration`.

The backend mistakes hide or misattribute failures. Using object names as kinds also creates an unbounded set of histogram label values. Correct these observations and assert backend labels and sample counts in tests.

findings.title: Shared mocks cannot verify either backend’s write behavior
findings.description:
Every subtest gives legacy and primary storage the same `mock.Mock`, and both adapters report identical method names through `m.Called`. Thus an expectation configured as “legacy” can satisfy a primary call. For example, the Create failure case configures only `setupLegacyFn`, yet that expectation supplies the primary-storage error.

The tests also neither wait for asynchronous replication nor assert its expectations. Delete and DeleteCollection success cases can reuse the primary expectation for the legacy call, so they do not independently verify replication.

Use separate backend mocks, synchronize background completion, and assert calls and results for each backend. Include primary failure, legacy failure, cancellation, and ordering cases.

structured_findings.summary: Background writes retain the request’s cancellation
Update recomputes the mutation against the legacy object
Independent goroutines can replicate writes out of order
Duration observations use the wrong backend and label
Shared mocks cannot verify either backend’s write behavior
